tldr: ArCHer is a hierarchical multi-turn reinforcement learning framework for fine-tuning LLMs that runs a high-level off-policy Q-learning algorithm and a low-level on-policy token-generation algorithm in parallel, achieving ~100x sample efficiency gains over on-policy methods like PPO.
contributions: A general framework (ArCHer: Actor-Critic Framework with a Hierarchical Structure) for developing multi-turn RL algorithms for LLMs that combines high-level utterance-level value learning with low-level token-level policy optimization
Formulation of language generation as a hierarchical MDP with utterance-level actions at the high level and token-level actions at the low level
Demonstration of ~100x sample efficiency improvement over PPO and convergence to better performance than off-policy methods, with effectiveness shown up to 7B parameter scale
methods: The framework poses multi-turn language generation as a hierarchical MDP where each turn/utterance is a high-level action and each token within a turn is a low-level action. Two RL algorithms run in parallel: a high-level off-policy TD learner trains utterance-level Q and V functions using Bellman backups over stored interaction data, while a low-level on-policy actor optimizes token generation via REINFORCE policy gradients using the Q-derived advantage as terminal reward. The approach can also be extended with a token-level baseline for variance reduction and adapted for offline RL training.
results: ArCHer achieves approximately 100x sample efficiency over existing on-policy methods like PPO, converges to better performance than off-policy methods, and scales effectively up to 7 billion parameters. For comparison, token-level ILQL took more than 10 days to converge on a task while filtered behavior cloning took less than a day.
limitations: The paper notes that off-policy utterance-level methods using multiple candidate utterances from frozen pre-trained LLMs reduce the pace of policy improvement
Token-level methods suffer from extremely long horizons resulting in slow learning speeds
Direct Q-value optimization in offline settings can result in overestimation, divergence, and poor policy performance (partially addressed but discussed as a challenge)
